title: {{NAME}} and the Crown of Silver Hooves
moral: True courage means speaking up for those who cannot speak for themselves.

pages.content: Beyond the last oak tree at the edge of {{NAME}}'s garden, where the grass grew soft as velvet and the fireflies blinked like tiny lanterns, lay the Moonpetal Meadow. It was the sort of place that made your breath catch and your feet slow to a reverent hush. Silver flowers trembled in a breeze that smelled of warm honey and rain. In the very centre of the meadow stood a unicorn, her coat the colour of fresh snow, her mane threaded with ribbons of pale violet light. Beside her, perched on a mossy stone, sat Princess Orla, a girl of perhaps eight with copper braids and a travelling cloak the shade of autumn leaves. She was crying quietly, her small shoulders shaking. {{NAME}} stepped through the gap in the hedge and stopped. Something was very, very wrong in this magical place.

pages.content: {{NAME}} crept closer, careful not to snap a single twig. The unicorn turned her great dark eyes toward him, and they were deep as mountain lakes, full of a sorrow that made his chest ache. Princess Orla looked up too, her cheeks streaked with silver tears that glittered strangely, almost like starlight. 'Who are you?' she whispered, not unkindly. {{NAME}} told her his name and asked, as gently as he could, what was the matter. Orla explained everything in a tumbling rush of words. The unicorn, whose name was Lunara, wore a golden crown tangled deep in her mane, placed there by the mischievous fox twins, Pip and Pox, who had thought it terribly funny. Now the crown was knotted tight as a sailor's rope, and every time Lunara tried to shake it free, it pulled her mane and stung her eyes. She had been standing still for hours, too proud to ask for help, too gentle to run.

pages.content: {{NAME}} did not waste a moment. He rolled up his sleeves, studied the knot the way he studied a puzzle, and began to work. It was trickier than it looked. The golden crown had looped itself three times around a thick braid, and each loop locked the others tighter. He teased one strand free, then another, his fingers nimble and patient. Princess Orla held Lunara's neck steady, murmuring a soft song her grandmother had taught her, a melody that made the unicorn's breathing slow and calm. The fox twins, Pip and Pox, crept back to the meadow edge, their amber eyes watching with growing shame. They had come to laugh, but something about {{NAME}}'s quiet determination and Orla's steady courage made laughter feel hollow. Loop by loop, the golden crown lifted free. Lunara tossed her mane with a sound like distant bells, and the silver flowers all around them burst into sudden, blazing bloom.

pages.content: Lunara lowered her great head and placed her spiralled horn gently against {{NAME}}'s forehead. A warmth spread through him like sunlight pouring into a cold room, and for one breathtaking moment he could hear every creature in the meadow — the beetles, the moths, the sleeping rabbits below the roots — all of them alive and content. Then Pip and Pox padded forward, their bushy tails low. 'We are sorry,' said Pip, in a voice smaller than {{NAME}} had expected. 'We did not think about how it felt,' said Pox. 'That,' said Princess Orla, stepping toward them with quiet grace, 'is exactly the thing you must always think about first.' The fox twins looked at one another, and something shifted in their amber eyes, something that had not been there before. Lunara pressed her nose to each fox's head in turn, forgiving them without a single word, and the meadow felt lighter, as though the whole night had exhaled.

pages.content: Lunara carried {{NAME}} and Orla once around the meadow on her back, her hooves barely touching the ground, each step leaving a brief shimmer of light in the silver grass. The fox twins trotted alongside, their tails now high and hopeful. When {{NAME}} finally slipped back through the gap in the hedge, the night air of his own garden felt different, warmer somehow, as if it remembered where he had been. He curled into bed, the sheets cool and soft, his eyes already heavy with the good tiredness that comes after doing something that truly matters. Princess Orla had promised to visit again. Lunara had left one small silver flower tucked into the hedge. And somewhere in the velvet dark beyond the garden, {{NAME}} was almost certain he could hear the faint, faraway sound of fox cubs laughing, but this time, with someone, not at someone. He smiled, closed his eyes, and wondered what he might find if he crept back through that hedge tomorrow night.
